learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how attitudes are formed, how they influence behavior, how they can be changed through persuasion, and how we interpret our social world!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: An attitude is a state of mind, a set of views or thoughts regarding a topic (attitude object). They are structured around the A-B-C model: Affective component (feelings/emotions), Behavioural component (actions), and Cognitive component (thoughts/beliefs).

Attitudes are learned through classical conditioning, operant conditioning, and modeling. Attitudes can change through persuasion or when cognitive dissonance occurs (when two cognitive elements are inconsistent, causing psychological discomfort).

Social cognition refers to how we process, store, and use information about other people. When we assign causes to people's behavior, it is called Attribution. We often make the 'Fundamental Attribution Error'—attributing others' behavior to internal traits while ignoring external situational factors.

Prejudice is a pre-conceived opinion or attitude (often negative) toward a group. When prejudice is translated into unfair actions, it becomes Discrimination. Stereotypes are generalized beliefs about a group.

fun_activity.title: 📺 Analyzing Advertising Persuasion
fun_activity.instructions: Watch a commercial on television or YouTube. Identify how it tries to change consumer attitudes: Does it rely on emotional appeal (Affective), logical facts (Cognitive), or celebrity endorsement? Spot the persuasion strategy!

exam_tips: 📌 Master the A-B-C model of attitudes (Affective, Behavioural, Cognitive)—a staple 2-mark question.
📌 Leon Festinger's theory of 'Cognitive Dissonance' and how people try to reduce inconsistency is frequently tested.
📌 Differentiate clearly between Stereotypes (beliefs), Prejudice (attitudes/feelings), and Discrimination (actions).
quick_recap: ⭐ Attitudes consist of affective, behavioural, and cognitive components (A-B-C model).
⭐ Cognitive dissonance explains how conflicting thoughts drive attitude change.
⭐ Social cognition shapes how we judge others, often prone to attribution errors and prejudices.
